As I was writing my umpteenth lettre de motivation in French, I wondered: how much of what a candidate can do, gets lost under the rules of a language they have yet to fully perfect?

I'm Malaysian of Chinese Peranakan descent. I grew up between Malay, English, Mandarin and Hokkien, and picked up Indonesian and Cantonese along the way. For the past 12 years, I've been sharing a life with my spouse, who's French. Now, my daily life is a constant navigation across Hofstede's cultural dimensions: when to be direct and when to keep the harmony, when to have everything planned and when to let things unfold naturally, as Lao Tzu would have it.

I came to realise that speaking several languages is not only about communicating fluently with different interlocutors. Rather, it is also about interpreting an idea from different perspectives, and knowing how to convey it to different audiences. Once you have lived that, you will look at a problem with multiple possibilities.

I'm of the opinion that this ability is more than a soft skill - it is a business advantage. I met a recruiter at the recent VivaTech 2026, who told me that they appreciate hiring Malaysians because of our multilingual and multicultural competencies. Multilinguals open doors to new markets and clients. They notice when the way of working in Paris will be counterproductive in Kuala Lumpur before it costs anything. They are the bridge between headquarters and local teams who would otherwise be talking past each other. A European Commission study of nearly 2,000 exporting SMEs found that 11% had lost a contract because of a lack of language skills. This shows that the cost of not having multilinguals is real.

Today, AI can polish anyone's cover letter in seconds, and that is a new problem in itself. LinkedIn's CEO recently said that recruiters are drowning in a sea of applications that look the same. What stands out now is a real perspective, shaped by real experiences. While I agree with this, when I think of job seekers looking for opportunities away from home, so much can get lost in translation when we operate in a language that we are still learning.

I think as long as the hiring process is still heavily automated, the qualities a team needs most might often not reach a human. What AI can do is translate our words, but it can't translate our judgement.

 💡 My wish for recruiters: before an application is screened out for imperfect French, give it one human read. What's missing in grammar may be more than made up for in perspective. Or ask questions like 'What have you learned from living between cultures, and how will you apply that to your role?' in applications, on top of language proficiency.

 📢 To my fellow multilinguals, how many languages do you speak, and what challenges have you faced applying for jobs away from home?

🔮 My honest AI predictions. Unpopular but real.

1. Every job in front of a screen will eventually disappear.

Customer support. Data entry. QA testing. Basic coding. Content writing.
If your entire job is clicking, typing and repeating — AI is coming for it.
Not tomorrow. But sooner than most people are comfortable admitting.

2. Developers will be rehired to clean up the mess AI made.

We've seen this movie before.
Offshore outsourcing promised cheaper, faster software.
It delivered — and then companies spent years fixing the technical debt.

AI is following the exact same script.
Businesses will ship fast with AI-generated code.
Then one day the system breaks, nobody understands why, and they'll desperately need a senior engineer who actually knows what's happening under the hood.

The irony? The developers AI displaced will be the ones called back to fix it.

3. The AI bubble will burst.

Not all of it. But enough to hurt.
Valuations are disconnected from reality.
Half the "AI startups" are wrappers around GPT with a nice UI.
When revenue doesn't match the hype — and it won't for many — the correction will be brutal.

The companies built on real AI integration will survive and thrive.
The ones built on AI theatre will vanish overnight.


Here's what I actually believe though —
AI isn't the end of human work.
It's the end of lazy, replaceable, low-skill work.

The developers who survive and thrive will be the ones who:
→ Understand systems deeply, not just syntax
→ Use AI as a force multiplier, not a crutch
→ Can clean up what AI gets wrong — and know why it got it wrong


I've been building with AI in production for years.
Not as a shortcut. As a multiplier.

The bubble may burst. The mess will need cleaning.
I'll still be here — building, leading and shipping.

Every company in India deploying an LLM now has a legal problem it has not priced.

The problem is not whether the model is good. The problem is what happens when it is wrong. A customer is misled. A loan is denied. A hiring decision is biased. A data subject's rights are ignored. A regulator asks a question the company cannot answer.

The lawyers inside these companies do not know what a context window is. The engineers do not know what the DPDPA requires. The gap between the two is where the liability sits.

The Advocacy — A Law Firm exists to close that gap.

Our focus is corporate litigation, insolvency and restructuring, and arbitration. Over the past year we have built a second practice area: data protection and AI governance.

The DPDPA compliance deadline is 13 May 2027. Full obligations take effect on that date. The Data Protection Board will begin adjudicating. Most Indian companies have not started.

We have built a retrieval-first legal engine called Unknown Verdict. It returns the verbatim text of an Indian statute, cited to the source PDF and page number. No generation in the retrieval path. No marginal cost per query. It is live at https://lnkd.in/dX8wBcvw, and published under our Article 39A commitment to equal access to justice.

We have authored a working paper titled Calculator, Not Mind: Anthropomorphic Language and the Risk of a Liability Shield for AI Developers. The paper argues that mental predicates applied to language models — "thinking," "reasoning," "refusing," "acting autonomously" — shift responsibility from the company that built the system to the tool itself. It is under review by legal practitioners before publication.

Services

We offer four defined engagements. Not hours. Deliverables.

AI Liability Audit. For companies deploying any AI system. A written report identifying where the company is exposed if the system produces a wrong output, who the legal doer is under current law, and what mitigations are required. Fixed fee.

DPDPA Readiness Assessment. A gap assessment across data processing, notice, consent, breach response, and Data Processing Agreements. Prioritised remediation plan with cost and timeline. Fixed fee.

DPO-as-a-Service. An outsourced Data Protection Officer for companies that require one but do not need a full-time hire. Monthly retainer. Recurring.

AI Governance Programme. For companies with multiple AI systems across jurisdictions. Ongoing policy stack review, contract drafting, incident response, board-level training. Monthly retainer.

We also provide fractional General Counsel support.


Our advisory work, our tools, and our research exist to remove that shield.

If your company is deploying AI, or processing personal data, and has not yet assessed its exposure, we should talk. The deadline is seven months away.

48% of US hiring managers would rather invest in AI tools than hire and train a recent grad.

I'm a recent grad. Fun read.

But the same survey says something else.

65% still plan to hire the same number of 2026 grads, or more.

Both can be true.

My read: entry-level jobs aren't vanishing. The bar for "entry-level" is moving.

Look at the other numbers:

→ 61% would only consider grads without an internship for certain roles, or not at all
→ 76% said new grads need help with basic documents like memos and contracts

Nobody is asking for more theory.

They're asking for proof you can do the work.

And honestly, this is where "entry-level" gets confusing.

If companies expect graduates to arrive with internships, projects and workplace experience, what exactly counts as entry-level anymore?

A degree says I can learn.

A project says I can do.

That's why I'm trying to build both.

Fewer jobs isn't the whole story. A higher bar is.

The conversation around Python in data engineering for 2026 is shifting from "Python is the glue language" to "Python is the orchestration language for agentic data systems." The most advanced pipelines I see in production are no longer collections of batch scripts stitched together by Airflow. They are event-driven, self-healing workflows where Python functions are compiled into lightweight, isolated execution units that react to schema drift, data quality thresholds, and cost anomalies in real-time.

The non-obvious implication is that the Python skills that matter most are not about writing faster pandas or cleaner Python. They are about designing type-safe data contracts that can be enforced at the boundary of every transformation. I have observed that teams using Python with Pydantic and strict type hints at the pipeline entry point reduce runtime failures by 40% compared to those relying on runtime assertions. The bottleneck is no longer execution speed; it is the discipline of schema-first design.

Another structural change is the commoditization of boilerplate ETL generation by AI. In 2026, any Python engineer can generate a transformation script in seconds. The differentiator is no longer the code itself but the observability layer that validates the generated code against production data contracts. The teams winning are the ones embedding Python-based validation rules into their CI/CD pipeline that reject AI-generated transformations if they produce semantic drift or violate lineage constraints.

For recruiters and hiring managers: I am not looking for a role that asks me to write Python scripts that move data from one bucket to another. I am seeking a problem where I can design the Python-based orchestration, validation, and governance frameworks that make data engineering predictable at scale. If your team is struggling with AI-generated pipeline code that introduces silent errors, or with Python-heavy pipelines that are brittle under schema evolution, I want to hear about the specific workload patterns and compliance requirements you are facing.

What is the one Python pattern in your current pipelines that, if replaced with a contract-first approach, would eliminate your most common production incident?

Let’s normalize giving candidates the option to submit their full resume.

After 25+ years in IT, I’ve stopped trying to squeeze my entire career into two pages. Too often, the projects removed to save space are the ones that explain what I can actually do.

A job title and three bullets can leave a lot unexplained: what someone designed, the problems they solved, the responsibilities they owned, and the results they delivered.

This applies early in a career, too. Projects, internships, contract work, and transferable experience deserve room when they help demonstrate someone’s abilities.

AI tools can help reviewers summarize a detailed resume, find experience relevant to a position, and identify useful interview questions. The supporting detail can remain available for anyone who wants to look deeper.

Put a useful summary up front. Organize the experience clearly. Give readers enough information to understand the candidate.

That’s the approach I’ve taken with my own resume: an overview first, followed by the work that supports it.

I’d like to see relevance and substance carry more weight than an arbitrary page count.

AI replacing only 5% of what we do does not mean the other 95% stays the same.

Mustafa Suleyman’s thought-provoking post on Daron Acemoglu’s essay in The Humanist Review raised a number of questions for me. Here are a few reflections from the perspective of a practitioner working inside a company.

Take contract review in a corporate legal team. AI may not replace a single lawyer. But once it handles the first draft and initial review, the job itself changes. The role may shift toward judgment and negotiation, while junior lawyers lose some of the routine work through which they have traditionally learned.

What happens to the time that is freed up? Is it redirected to other work and new roles, or used to reduce headcount or hiring?

That is a management choice, shaped by business strategy, cost pressures and investor expectations. The technology itself does not decide.

I strongly share the aspiration to build AI that makes people better at what they do. But augmentation is an aspiration, not an automatic outcome.

One point highlighted in Suleyman’s post is that incentives matter. If tax and economic structures favour automation over labour, firms may be pushed toward replacement even when augmentation could create greater long-term value.

Timing matters too.

Slower adoption does not necessarily mean smaller impact. It may mean a longer period of asymmetry, in which those who organise around AI earlier gain disproportionate capabilities and influence. Given AI’s general-purpose nature, that asymmetry could be profound.

The real question, then, is whether we can design institutions, incentives and governance that favour augmentation while AI capabilities advance faster than our institutions can adapt.

How are others thinking about the balance between augmentation, automation and institutional design in their own organisations?
